metadata.title: ECIS — Episode 14: Knowing What You Don't Know

beats.narration_text: Thirteen episodes of teaching a system to read earnings calls. This one teaches it the thing experts take longest to learn: when to say nothing at all. I'm Anjana.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself

props.command: ECIS answers every time it is asked, and some of those answers are worth less than the others. Can it put an honest interval around each prediction, refuse the ones it can't stand behind, notice when one company's language starts showing up in its peers, and take a question in plain English?

beats.narration_text: ECIS extracts guidance signals from earnings call transcripts using four readers — keyword, FinBERT, NER, and LLM — weighted by a five-dimension triangulator. A six-model ensemble predicts guidance revisions. Calibrated confidence scores, contradiction detection, and SHAP explanations tell you not just what the system predicts, but why — and an out-of-distribution detector flags transcripts the models haven't seen before. This week, the system learns something new: when not to answer at all.

props.sparkLine: This week: when not to answer.

beats.narration_text: Instead of a single number, every prediction now comes with a confidence band. Conformal prediction wraps each forecast in a distribution-free interval — seventy-two percent likely to revise, but the true probability sits somewhere between sixty-one and eighty-three. Monte Carlo dropout runs fifty forward passes with dropout active, measuring how much the prediction wobbles. And ensemble disagreement tracks whether all six models agree or scatter. Three lenses on the same question: how sure are we, really?

When all three uncertainty measures spike — wide intervals, high dropout variance, models disagreeing — the system does something unusual. It abstains. Rather than force a low-confidence forecast, it flags the prediction as unreliable and steps aside. About twelve percent of predictions trigger abstention. The payoff: accuracy on the remaining eighty-eight percent improves by eight points. Knowing when to say I don't know turns out to be its own kind of intelligence.

Signals don't stay inside one company. When a sector leader starts hedging, peers often follow within one or two quarters. The system now tests for this using Granger causality across every company pair in a sector, building a contagion map of who leads and who lags. It extends to supply chains too — when a supplier's language deteriorates, customers downstream tend to shift one to two quarters later. One company's signal becomes another company's early warning.

All of this is now queryable in natural language. An agentic layer built on LangGraph decomposes questions into sub-tasks, routes them to the right tools — signal retrieval, cross-company analytics, SHAP explanations — and synthesizes structured responses. Ask which companies show deterioration signals, and the agent scans the full corpus. Ask why a particular company was flagged, and it pulls the SHAP attributions. The system doesn't just compute — it converses.

props.sparkLine: It doesn't just compute — it converses.

beats.narration_text: Nineteen phases in, the system now quantifies its own uncertainty, abstains when it should, tracks how language shifts propagate across companies and supply chains, and answers questions about everything it knows. The most important upgrade wasn't a new model or a new feature. It was teaching the system to say: I'm not confident enough to call this one. Next week, we keep building.

Let's recap with Claude. Thirteen episodes built a system that answers. This one gives it the option not to. Every prediction now carries an interval rather than a point, measured three different ways, because one measure of uncertainty is a guess about a guess. When all three widen at once the system abstains — it hands back no answer rather than a bad one, on about an eighth of cases, and the answers it does give get better. It also stopped treating companies as independent: when a sector leader starts hedging, the system now tests whether its peers follow, and how many quarters behind. And all of it can be asked a question in plain English.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the uncomfortable one. Almost every model in production is forced to answer every time it's asked, including the times it has no business answering. Paste this into Claude and work out what your own abstention rule would be — what you'd measure, where you'd set the threshold, and who gets the case when the model steps aside.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself

props.command: I run a model that has to answer every time it is asked, and I suspect some of those answers are worthless. Can you help me: one, work out which measures of uncertainty my model can actually produce — intervals, sampling variance, disagreement between models — and which of those I can get cheaply; two, design an abstention rule and tell me how to pick its threshold from my own risk–coverage curve rather than guessing; and three, tell me honestly what has to happen to a case after the model steps aside, because if the answer is nothing then abstention is just a slower failure.
